The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional arc of the narrative. The author uses **compression of time** at the very beginning, summarizing a four-mile walk and years of marital history into just two brief paragraphs. Time is also compressed during the physical exertion of CPR ("Eventually his arms would not straighten"), allowing the reader to quickly bypass the procedural failure and get to the emotional core of the story.

Once it is clear the woman cannot be saved, the author shifts to **stretching of time** (or slowing the pace down) as Martin waits for the rescue team. During this period of stillness, the narrative expands through Martin's hyper-fixation on small physical details (a loose bootlace, a bag of oranges, a silver ring, pale wood through bark) and delves deep into his internal thoughts and memories (his career, his strained phone call with his son, his dying mother). This slowing down of time mirrors the quiet, heavy reality of sitting with a body in the woods, giving Martin the narrative space he needs to reflect on his own stubbornness and isolation, which makes his final decision to reach out to his son feel completely earned.
